extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of journalism, media studies researchers, and journalism educators
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and analyze Warren Breed's account of how newsroom 'policy' is transmitted and enforced, the social mechanisms producing journalist compliance, conditions for deviation, and the ethical and social consequences of those processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy learned through newsroom socialization
rubrics_metrics.description: New journalists learn the newsroom 'policy' informally as they learn the job and discover how the newsroom works and what its values are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed lists concrete socialization mechanisms: reading their own paper (shows what gets on page one), editing of their stories, reprimands and compliments, gossip with staff and editors, informal news 'conferences', house organs/newsletters, and observation of executives and hearing their comments. Policy is almost never written down; it is inferred from routine cues and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional authority and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional authority and the fear of sanctions compel journalists to comply with policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed notes that fear of sanctions is 'usually enough' to enforce policy; editors themselves may be unsure of explicit policy and act on their perception of it, reinforcing compliance through hierarchical authority rather than written rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feelings of obligation and esteem for superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: New journalists develop gratitude and esteem for those who hired and mentored them, fostering compliance with perceived policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This factor functions via personal ties and mentorship: journalists form good working relationships with immediate superiors from whom they continue to learn and who assign work, making them reluctant to challenge policy set by those superiors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambition as a compliance mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal ambition—seeking advancement and front-page placement—encourages journalists to avoid stories that conflict with policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed points out that getting ahead requires publishing desirable stories; journalists avoid work they believe will be suppressed or penalized, aligning behavior with what is perceived to lead to career success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of conflicting group allegiance (weak professional organizations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of strong external professional organizations leaves journalists without an alternative source of values or loyalties, increasing internal compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed cites low membership in professional associations (e.g., only 7% belonged to SPJ in his data) as evidence that journalists have few organized external allegiances to counter newsroom policy. This absence reduces incentives to defy management on principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasant team-oriented work environment
rubrics_metrics.description: A congenial, team-like newsroom atmosphere makes journalists inclined to conform with policy to belong and keep work enjoyable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed notes that feeling part of the team and finding the work interesting reduces tendency to challenge policy; pleasant nature of the work is itself a social control mechanism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of 'getting the news' as a controlling value
rubrics_metrics.description: The professional habit of privileging news-gathering above policy or ideological questions causes journalists to set aside policy conflicts when there is news to get.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: 'News comes first....' (p.117, Compass). Breed argues that even when journalists talk about ethics or objectivity, those concerns are often suspended in favor of pursuing news, which reinforces compliance with routines that facilitate rapid reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom morale influences policy compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The overall morale of a newsroom affects how strictly policy is followed: high morale correlates with fewer policy conflicts, low morale with more resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed found five of the six compliance factors present in all studied newsrooms; esteem for superiors varied. Where morale was high, journalists were less likely to buck policy; where morale was low, they tended to resist policy more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical constraint: policy and law collapse ethical agency ('good employee' model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional policy and media law operate as constraints that make ethical violations as difficult to justify as legal ones, producing a 'good employee' model of ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed (and Demers commentary) argue that ethical consciousness routinely collapses into policy compliance—'Do not rock the boat, comply with policies and do not break the law.' This model is critiqued as falling short of a professional ideal of ethics because it privileges employer directives over independent ethical judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions enabling policy deviation
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy can be bypassed in contexts where policy is unclear, where individual journalists have strong expertise, or where situational factors reduce enforcement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific enabling conditions listed by Breed: unclear or unwritten policies; journalist becomes an 'expert' in an area lacking clear policy; another media outlet publishes a story after a leak; initiative stories or beat stories; 'star' journalists who can usually ignore policy. These are zones where 'real' journalism can occur despite formal policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pathways for policy change
rubrics_metrics.description: Meaningful change in newsroom policy is most likely to come from external pressures on publishers and strengthened professional codes of ethics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed's conclusion: 'Any important change toward a more free and responsible press must stem from various possible pressures on the publisher, who epitomises the policy making and coordinating role' (p.120). He suggests pressure from readers and enforceable/professional ethical standards as change mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy's social effect: protection of property/class interests and selective reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Newsroom policy tends to protect property and class interests, which can result in slanting or burying policy-relevant news and denying important information to the citizenry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Breed argues that 'policy usually protects property and class interests' and that while much news is printed objectively allowing opinion to form, 'policy news may be slanted or buried' so some important information is withheld from the public. This frames policy as a structural influence on news content with normative consequences.
